UPDATE course_lessons SET content = CONCAT(content, '

## Real-World Diagnostic Scenario: The Single-Phasing Motor

**Situation:** A 25HP, 480V, 3-phase squirrel-cage induction motor driving a centrifugal pump in a water treatment plant starts making a loud humming/growling noise and the amp clamp shows 45A on Phase A, 0A on Phase B, and 44A on Phase C. The motor is running but at reduced speed and the frame temperature is climbing rapidly. The overload hasn''t tripped yet because it''s a melting-alloy type with a 10-second delay.

**Diagnostic Thinking:**

1. **Identify the symptom pattern:** Two phases carrying high current, one phase at zero = classic single-phasing condition. The motor has lost one phase of its 3-phase supply.
2. **Why is it still running?** A 3-phase induction motor that is already spinning when it loses a phase will continue to run on the remaining two phases. However, it now operates as a single-phase motor with a pulsating (not rotating) magnetic field component. The rotor must work much harder, drawing approximately $\sqrt{3}$ times normal current on the remaining two phases.
3. **Why the noise?** The pulsating magnetic field component creates a strong 120Hz vibration (twice line frequency) that produces the characteristic growl.
4. **Immediate action:** STOP the motor immediately. Continued operation will overheat the stator windings (the current is concentrated in 2/3 of the winding) and destroy the insulation within minutes.

**Finding the Root Cause:**

| Check Point | Tool | Expected Finding |
|---|---|---|
| Motor terminal box | Multimeter (VAC) | 480V A-C, 0V A-B, 0V B-C → confirms Phase B lost upstream |
| MCC bucket | Multimeter (VAC) | Check line side of contactor — if Phase B is present here but not at motor, contactor has a welded/open contact |
| Upstream fuse/breaker | Visual + multimeter | One blown fuse in the MCC bucket feeder (most common cause) |

**Most Common Causes of Single-Phasing:**
- Blown fuse on one phase (often due to a downstream ground fault that cleared itself)
- Welded or pitted contactor contact that finally opened
- Loose wire on a terminal block that vibrated free
- Utility-side issue (rare in industrial plants with redundant feeds)

> **Technician Tip:** Modern electronic overloads (like Allen-Bradley E1 Plus or Siemens 3RB series) detect single-phasing within 2-3 seconds and trip immediately. If your plant still has melting-alloy overloads on critical motors, recommend upgrading to electronic overloads — the motor you save could cost $15,000+ to rewind.') WHERE id = 19;
